title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

reading.body:
This is an impersonation failure built on synthetic media. An AI-generated video presented a well-known financial sector personality as the face of an investment, and the victim treated the apparent endorsement as evidence that the offer was real. The model or tool did not assert a false fact in text; it manufactured a person's likeness and voice into a testimonial that person had not given. The false claim was carried by the video itself, and the fraud depended on the victim accepting the likeness as proof of the person's involvement.

The AI video was only the entry point. The rest of the scheme ran through ordinary channels: a small initial investment, then contact on WhatsApp, pressure to pay more, instructions to open multiple online accounts, and remote access to the victim's computer given on the claim that it would help with the investment. The victim was encouraged to borrow money to keep investing, and the funds went to accounts controlled by criminals. Catching it would have required a check that the person in the video had any connection to the investment, and a check that the provider was authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority. Neither check is described as having happened before the money moved.

What is not established is the identity of the celebrity, whom the Police Service of Northern Ireland did not name. No arrest, charge or verdict appears in the reporting, and the account of the loss rests on the police statement rather than on a court finding. Whether the person depicted had any knowledge of or involvement in the video is not established.

reports.title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

summary:
A person in the Ards and north Down area lost £250,000 in an AI-generated investment scam, the Police Service of Northern Ireland said. The victim saw an AI video featuring a well-known financial sector personality, which promoted an investment with claimed significant returns. After a small initial investment, the victim was contacted on WhatsApp and urged to pay more. The fraudsters had the victim create multiple online accounts and gave them remote access to the computer, saying they were helping with the investment.

Police called it a sophisticated and substantial fraud. The victim was encouraged to borrow money to keep investing, and funds went to accounts controlled by criminals. The PSNI did not name the celebrity, though BBC News NI has seen similar scams using financial experts Martin Lewis, Peter Jones and Steven Bartlett. Superintendent Joanne Gibson, chair of the Scamwise Partnership, urged people to stop and check financial activity and to talk with relatives about fraud. Police advised verifying who they are dealing with and checking that financial services providers are authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority.
